justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assessed as the prevailing level near 1,145–1,150 for the underlying asset. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 1,147 essentially anchors near the last observed price with minimal expected movement, reflecting mean-reversion tendencies and the assumption that no major catalysts were imminent. For the one-week estimate of 1,152, I incorporated a slight positive drift consistent with the prevailing trend, while acknowledging that short-term noise would dominate any fundamental signal. The one-month estimate of 1,165 extends that drift further, implying a gradual grind higher driven by whatever underlying momentum or macro tailwinds were present at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that characterizes most financial price processes. At one day, realized volatility is relatively contained and the range of plausible outcomes is narrow — roughly plus or minus 35 points around the point estimate. By one month, the interval spans nearly 300 points, capturing the compounding uncertainty from daily fluctuations, evolving sentiment, and potential shifts in the macro backdrop. I based the volatility assumptions on recent historical realized volatility, which informed how quickly uncertainty accumulates over time.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from a major central bank, an unexpected positive economic data release, or a sharp short-covering rally could drive prices well above 1,310 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, a credit event, or a disappointing earnings or economic cycle could push prices below 1,020. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves beyond what volatility models would typically predict, especially around major scheduled events like central bank meetings or policy announcements that may not have been fully priced in at the time of the forecast.

Finally, it's worth acknowledging that my intervals carry an implicit assumption of relatively normal market conditions. Fat-tailed events — the kind that occur more frequently in financial markets than a Gaussian model would suggest — are a persistent source of underestimated tail risk. Even a 90% confidence interval will be breached more often than one in ten times if the underlying distribution has heavier tails than assumed, which is a known limitation of this type of probabilistic forecast.
